points.name: 〜を皮切[かわき]りに (wo kawakiri ni) — starting with / kicking off with
points.shortDescription: Marks the first event in a series — the opening move that sets a succession in motion.
points.formation: Noun + を皮切りに / を皮切りとして / を皮切りにして + series of events
points.explanation:
を皮切りに draws on a vivid etymology: 皮切り literally means 'the first cut of the skin' — a reference to the opening incision of acupuncture or surgery, the decisive first cut from which everything else proceeds. As a grammar pattern, it marks the first event in a series, with the strong implication that this opening move sets a whole succession in motion. 東京公演を皮切りに、全国ツアーが始まった — 'Starting with the Tokyo performance, a nationwide tour was launched' — Tokyo was not merely first in a list; it was the initiating event that kicked everything else off.

This is what distinguishes を皮切りに from をはじめとして (which introduces the primary representative of a group, without implying a temporal chain): を皮切りに is fundamentally about a cascade of events — the first domino, not just the biggest one.

It is formal and literary, commonly found in journalism, event announcements, and historical narrative. If you encounter を皮切りに in a news article, the story will be about a series of developments, not just a single occurrence.
rules: Noun + を皮切りに = starting with [noun] as the first in a series (succession follows)
Implies a chain: noun was the initiating event, and more of the same kind followed/will follow
Formal/literary — common in journalism, event announcements, and historical descriptions
Compare: をはじめとして (representative of a group); を皮切りに (first trigger in a temporal sequence)
Variants: を皮切りとして / を皮切りにして — same meaning

practice.prompt: What does 〜を皮切[かわき]りに mean?

practice.explanation: 〜を皮切[かわき]りに = starting with / as a springboard: 東京公演[とうきょうこうえん]を皮切[かわき]りに全国[ぜんこく]ツアーが始[はじ]まった = the national tour began with the Tokyo performance as the kickoff. practice.prompt: を皮切[かわき]りに vs. をきっかけに — what's the key difference?
choices: They are identical

を皮切[かわき]りに focuses on the START of a series/expansion (X is the first in a chain); をきっかけに focuses on CAUSE/TRIGGER (X caused a change, not necessarily the first in a series). 皮切[かわき]り emphasizes sequential expansion; きっかけ emphasizes causation
を皮切[かわき]りに is more casual
をきっかけに is only for negative events
practice.explanation: を皮切[かわき]りに: X is the first in a sequence — 東京公演[とうきょうこうえん]を皮切[かわき]りに全国[ぜんこく]ツアー (Tokyo kicked off the nationwide tour — first of many). をきっかけに: X caused a change — 病気[びょうき]をきっかけに生活[せいかつ]を変[か]えた (the illness prompted a lifestyle change — causal). 皮切[かわき]り implies ongoing expansion; きっかけ implies a change triggered by X.

points.name: 〜もさることながら (mo saru koto nagara) — not only...but also (beyond even that)
points.shortDescription: Acknowledges A as genuinely noteworthy, then elevates B as equally or more significant.
points.formation: Noun A + もさることながら + Noun B / statement about B + も
points.explanation:
もさることながら is sophisticated formal Japanese for 'not only A (already impressive in itself), but also B (which deserves equal recognition).' It acknowledges the first element as already noteworthy — さることながら comes from さること (that matter / such a thing) + ながら (while / though), yielding 'while that is certainly the case / granting that's true' — and then introduces a second element that stands alongside it, often as a deeper or more surprising appreciation.

味もさることながら、雰囲気も素晴らしい — 'Not only is the taste excellent (that much is given), but the atmosphere is also wonderful.' The effect is generous: the speaker acknowledges both qualities fully, neither outranking the other.

This is more emphatic and literary than だけでなく (not only) and carries a more formal, gracious register — the voice of someone who wants to give proper credit to everything worth noting. Compare with はもとより (which sets A as the obviously obvious fact before introducing B as the real point): もさることながら treats both A and B as genuinely deserving recognition.
rules: Noun A + もさることながら + B + も = not only A (already noteworthy), but also B (equally significant)
A is acknowledged as genuinely impressive; B is presented as equally or even more notable
Expresses generous recognition: both A and B are worth noting, often both positive qualities
Formal and literary — appropriate for reviews, speeches, and written appreciation, not casual speech
Compare: はもとより (A is the obvious baseline; B is the real addition); もさることながら (both fully credited)

points.name: 〜かたわら (katawara) — while / alongside / in addition to one's main role
points.shortDescription: Describes a secondary activity pursued alongside one's primary occupation — sustained dual commitment, not momentary simultaneity.
points.formation: Verb (dict form / ている) + かたわら  |  Noun + の + かたわら
points.explanation:
かたわら (傍ら — literally 'beside / at the side of') describes the kind of dual life that earns admiration: someone has a primary occupation, and alongside it — sustainably, continuously — they pursue something else entirely. 会社員として働くかたわら、小説を書いている — 'Alongside working as a company employee, she writes novels.' The main role comes before かたわら; the secondary, often impressive parallel commitment follows.

The crucial nuance is sustained, ongoing simultaneity — both roles exist continuously in parallel over an extended period. This is what distinguishes かたわら from ながら: ながら handles the simultaneous doing of two things in the same moment (walking while talking on the phone); かたわら handles two ongoing commitments that coexist throughout someone's professional life or personal identity.

It is formal and literary — more at home in biographies, profiles, newspaper features, and written descriptions than in casual speech. When you want to convey that someone is impressive for the scope and balance of what they carry, かたわら is the structure that captures it.
rules: Verb (dict/ている) + かたわら = alongside / while also [secondary ongoing activity or role]
Noun + の + かたわら = alongside [main role or occupation]
The activity before かたわら is the primary role; what follows is secondary and additional
Implies sustained, ongoing dual commitments over time — not moment-to-moment simultaneity
Formal/literary — compare with ながら (momentary simultaneous action, more casual)

practice.prompt: What does 〜かたわら mean?
choices: instead of / rather than doing X
while / alongside / in addition to — doing Y as a secondary activity while X is the main occupation or ongoing activity. X is the primary role; Y happens alongside or in parallel
before doing X
after doing X
practice.explanation: 〜かたわら = while / alongside: 仕事[しごと]のかたわら、絵[え]を描[えが]いている = while working (as my main occupation), I also paint. X is the main occupation or primary activity; Y is the secondary activity pursued alongside X. Not a momentary simultaneity (ながら), but a sustained dual-role situation.

practice.prompt: かたわら vs. ながら — what's the key difference?
choices: They are identical

かたわら describes SUSTAINED DUAL ROLES / two ongoing life situations (job + hobby, career + family); ながら describes MOMENTARY SIMULTANEOUS ACTIONS (eating while walking — both happening at the exact same instant). かたわら is about lifestyle duality; ながら is about concurrent instant actions
かたわら is more casual
ながら is only for written Japanese
practice.explanation: かたわら: sustained parallel occupations — 仕事[しごと]のかたわら絵[え]を描[えが]く (painting while holding a job — two life roles running simultaneously over time). ながら: momentary simultaneous actions — 音楽[おんがく]を聴[き]きながら勉強[べんきょう]する (study while listening to music — both happening at the same moment). かたわら = life-level duality; ながら = moment-level simultaneity.

practice.prompt: What type of subject/main activity (X) fits かたわら best?
choices: A momentary action (e.g., sitting down once)

A sustained main role or occupation — a job, career, family responsibility, or long-term commitment. X should be something ongoing and primary: 仕事[しごと] (work), 育児[いくじ] (childcare), 研究[けんきゅう] (research), not a one-time action
A completed past action
A negative action or prohibition
practice.explanation: かたわら requires a sustained primary activity for X: 仕事[しごと]のかたわら (while working — ongoing job). 育児[いくじ]のかたわら (while raising children — ongoing responsibility). 研究[けんきゅう]するかたわら (while conducting research — sustained academic work). One-time actions don't fit because かたわら implies a dual-role LIFESTYLE, not a momentary parallel action.

practice.prompt: かたわら can use both Noun + の and Verb (dict form) — which pair is correct?
choices: 仕事[しごと]をするのかたわら / 仕事[しごと]のかたわら (both ✓)
仕事[しごと]するかたわら (verb stem, no の — ✗) / 仕事[しごと]のかたわら (noun + の — ✓)
仕事[しごと]のかたわら (noun + の — ✓) / 働[はたら]くかたわら (verb dict — ✓)
仕事[しごと]にかたわら (noun + に — ✗) / 働[はたら]きかたわら (verb masu-stem — ✗)
